passage: In the school gym in Valencia, the basketball coach pinned up the shooting stats. Next to Alejandro's name: "Missed 40%." He read it and felt his chest drop. That evening he told Freya he was thinking of quitting the team. "Forty percent failure, Freya. That's almost half." Freya pulled up her own sheet on her phone. On the girls' team sheet, the coach had written each player's number the other way round: "Scored 60%." "Your number's the same as mine," she said. "I felt great about mine." Alejandro stared at the two sheets. "Sixty percent sounds... good, actually." He stopped talking about quitting.

qa.q: What did the sheet say next to Alejandro's name?
qa.a: The sheet said "Missed 40%."

qa.q: Why did Alejandro think of quitting the team?
qa.a: Seeing his result written as a 40 percent failure made it feel like almost half was bad, which dragged his mood down and nearly his choice with it.

qa.q: What habit could help Alejandro when he sees a percentage like this?
qa.a: He could rewrite it both ways, missed and scored, before reacting, so the wording doesn't make his decisions for him.

qa.q: How might Freya feel about having the same number and feeling great?
qa.a: Freya may be amused and a little surprised that the same result could make one friend proud and the other ready to quit.

grounding: Shows a teenage boy ready to quit over a result worded as 40 percent missed, until the same figure framed as 60 percent scored changes his mood.

passage: At the coaching institute, the mock-test results appeared on the corridor screen: "Dhruv: 40% incorrect." Dhruv went pale and walked straight past the canteen. In the counselling room, Sarita ma'am found him staring at the floor. "I'm failing, ma'am. Forty percent wrong." She turned her laptop toward him. "Look at your printed report card instead." It said: "Accuracy 60%. Batch average 52%." Dhruv read it twice. "That's the same test?" "Same test, same you." "Then why does the screen say it like that?" Sarita ma'am sighed. "Someone chose that wording. Your reaction came from the words, not from the score." Dhruv looked a little less pale.

qa.q: What was the batch average on the printed report card?
qa.a: The batch average was 52%.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv go pale and skip the canteen?
qa.a: Dhruv felt ashamed and worried because the screen framed his result as 40% incorrect, so it felt like failing. That wording, not the score itself, sank his mood.

qa.q: What could the institute change about how results are shown?
qa.a: It could show accuracy and the batch average together, or both correct and incorrect, so students don't react to one gloomy word.

qa.q: How might Sarita ma'am feel about the corridor screen?
qa.a: Sarita ma'am seems frustrated with the wording, since it made a student feel he was failing when his score was above average.

grounding: Shows a teenage boy crushed by a result worded as 40 percent incorrect until he sees the same score framed as 60 percent accuracy.

passage:
Dear Ramesh chacha,
You asked how the science practicals went. The sheet says I failed 40% of the practical tasks. I was so upset that I told Mummy I'd drop science after Class 10. Then my friend's sheet from the other section said, "Completed 60% of practical tasks successfully." Same school, same practicals, same kind of result. She looked happy with hers! When I read mine again as "60% successful", it felt totally different, like I'm getting there. I haven't decided about science yet, but I'm not so sure I want to drop it now. Weird how one line can change a whole plan, no?
Your nephew,
Jatin

qa.q: What did Jatin's friend's sheet say?
qa.a: It said, "Completed 60% of practical tasks successfully."

qa.q: Why did Jatin tell Mummy he'd drop science?
qa.a: Jatin was so upset because the sheet framed the result as failing 40%, and that feeling pushed him toward a big decision.

qa.q: What would you advise Jatin before deciding about science?
qa.a: Look at the result both ways and ask the teacher what the 60% shows about his strengths and what to practise, then decide on that, not on the wording.

qa.q: How might Ramesh chacha respond to this letter?
qa.a: Ramesh chacha might feel relieved that Jatin noticed the wording effect, and suggest waiting before any big decision.

grounding: Shows a teenage boy whose mood and plans swing on whether his result is worded as 40 percent failed or 60 percent successful.

passage:
Honestly, Gopika, I nearly quit robotics over one word. Our first rover had to finish ten tasks at the inter-school round. It did six. Then the results sheet came, and next to our team it said: "Failure rate: 40%." I read that and my face went hot. I went home, told my parents robotics was a waste of time, and almost deleted all my code that night. I actually typed a message to the club leaving the group.
Next morning, Das sir stopped me in the corridor. "Arnab, young man, your rover passed sixty percent on its very first build. Most teams manage less." Same number, right? Six out of ten. But hearing it his way, my shoulders dropped and I thought, okay, four tasks to fix. I deleted the message instead of the code. We start rebuilding the steering on Saturday.

qa.q: What did the results sheet say next to Arnab's team?
qa.a: It said: "Failure rate: 40%."

qa.q: Why did 'failure rate' push Arnab towards quitting, even though the rover did six tasks?
qa.a: The word 'failure' made the whole result feel like proof he was bad at robotics, so leaving felt like a sensible way to stop the embarrassment.

qa.q: What was the turning point that changed Arnab's choice?
qa.a: Das sir described the same result as sixty percent passed on a first build, which let Arnab see four tasks to fix, so he deleted the message instead of the code.

qa.q: How might Gopika react while listening to Arnab's story?
qa.a: Gopika might be surprised that one line on a sheet almost ended something Arnab cares about, and might think twice about how the same number sounds when it is written two ways.

grounding: It shows a teenager reacting strongly when a result is called a 40 percent failure, and changing his choice when it is described as 60 percent success.

passage:
I'm Leela, and I share a wall with my brother Manav, so I hear most things. Last week his football academy posted fitness results in the team group. Beside his name: "Failed 4 of 10 drills." He didn't come out for dinner. The next two mornings his boots stayed by the door, and when Mummy asked, he said he was "done with football." I don't know what he was telling himself in there, but the door stayed shut.
On Thursday Seema ma'am, the coach, sent the players a voice note. I heard it through the wall: "Manav, six out of ten drills cleared in your first test this season. Build on that."
Ten minutes later he was lacing his boots. By the weekend he had signed up for the extra Saturday session. Same four drills, same six. Only the sentence was different.

qa.q: How many drills did Manav fail according to the team group post?
qa.a: He "Failed 4 of 10 drills."

qa.q: What might Manav have been thinking while his door stayed shut?
qa.a: He likely felt ashamed and discouraged, reading 'failed' as a verdict on himself, which is why quitting football seemed reasonable to him.

qa.q: How could the academy share results so players make steadier choices?
qa.a: It could state both sides at once, such as six cleared and four to work on, so one word does not swing a player's mood and decisions.

qa.q: How does Leela see what happened to Manav that week?
qa.a: From next door, Leela noticed that the same result produced two opposite reactions, and Leela seems both worried and struck that only the sentence was different.

grounding: Told by a sister, it shows a teenage boy swinging from quitting to extra practice depending on whether his result was worded as failure or success.
